docRefs.title: Python 3
docRefs.citedText: An interpreted language with a large standard library, readable syntax and no build step.

docRefs.title: Lox (Crafting Interpreters)
docRefs.citedText: A small dynamic teaching language from the free book Crafting Interpreters, built twice there, as a tree-walker and as a bytecode VM.

brief.summary: A tree-walking Lox interpreter written in stdlib Python, following Crafting Interpreters' structure. It stays small, runs in the browser via Pyodide, and is tested by a corpus of Lox programs from step 1.

layers.name: Python 3
layers.whatItIs: A readable interpreted language with a large standard library and no build step.
layers.roleHere: Implements every stage of the Lox interpreter, using only the standard library.
layers.whyChosen: Beats Rust because there is no borrow checker to fight, and beats Java or C, the book's languages, because you translate ideas rather than boilerplate. Stdlib-only code also runs in the browser.
pros: Stdlib-only code runs in the browser
cons: Types only checked by optional tools
layers.learnerCost: Classes, dataclasses, exceptions, and file I/O.

alternatives.name: Rust
alternatives.pickWhen: You want speed and are willing to learn ownership

alternatives.name: JavaScript
alternatives.pickWhen: The interpreter is a web-first project

assumptions: You use only the standard library

layers.name: Recursive descent parser
layers.whatItIs: A parser where each grammar rule is a function that calls other rule functions.
layers.roleHere: Turns Lox tokens into expression and statement trees, with precedence levels as functions.
layers.whyChosen: Beats ANTLR because it adds no tool or generated code and matches the book's approach. Beats a full Pratt parser because plain precedence functions are easier to read at first.
layers.learnerCost: Reading a grammar and turning each rule into a function.

alternatives.name: Pratt parser
alternatives.pickWhen: You want fewer functions for operators

assumptions: You follow the book's Lox grammar unchanged

layers.name: Tree-walking evaluator
layers.whatItIs: An evaluator that runs a program by visiting each node of its syntax tree.
layers.roleHere: Executes Lox statements and expressions directly from the tree, with environments for variables and closures.
layers.whyChosen: Beats a bytecode VM because it is far less code and Python's speed would waste a VM's benefits. Beats code generation because it needs no target toolchain.
pros: Closures and classes map to Python objects
cons: Deep Lox recursion can hit Python's limit
layers.learnerCost: The visitor pattern, environments, and exceptions for control flow.

alternatives.name: Bytecode VM
alternatives.pickWhen: You want the book's second half

assumptions: Following the book's first (tree-walking) half only

layers.name: File-based Lox test corpus
layers.whatItIs: A folder of Lox programs, each with its expected output and exit code.
layers.roleHere: tests/programs/ holds .lox files with expected stdout and exit code, run by a Python script after every step, including programs that must fail with specific messages.
layers.whyChosen: Beats unittest-only tests because the corpus is language-level and could check any implementation. Beats pytest because the stdlib is enough and keeps things browser-friendly.
pros: Fixed grammar means tests exist from step 1
Checks error messages and exit codes
layers.learnerCost: Subprocess calls, file layout, and exit-code conventions.
assumptions: Expected files sit next to each program, such as .out and .exit files

architecture.style: Pipeline: source to tokens to tree to evaluation, with a test runner around it.

components.name: Recursive descent parser
components.purpose: Builds the tree from Lox tokens.

components.name: Test corpus runner
components.purpose: Runs Lox programs and compares output and exit codes.

brief.howItFitsTogether: The test runner starts the interpreter on a .lox file. The source is split into tokens, the recursive descent parser builds a tree, and the evaluator walks it, printing output. The runner then compares stdout and the exit code to the expected files.
risks: Python's recursion limit breaks deeply recursive Lox programs
Translating the book's Java code line by line gives unidiomatic Python
Scope and closure bugs show up late
friction: The book's code is Java and C, so you translate rather than copy
Lox is dynamically typed, so there is no type checking stage to practise
